text:
A: Hello. Can you hear me alright?
B: Yes, hello. I am Tomasz, Warrington.
A: Imran, Huddersfield. Same motorway, then, more or less. The M62.
B: Ah, the M62. Every morning to Salford I sit on it. It is my enemy.
A: Ha. I'm on the A62 into town, which is no better, honestly. What takes you to Salford?
B: University. Civil engineering, second year. I am forty-four, so I am the old student.
A: Oh, that's brilliant, though. I did my qualifications in my thirties, evenings and online. Not a degree, mind. CompTIA, a Microsoft certificate. I'm in IT support.
B: So you also studied when everybody else was finished.
A: Sort of, yes. It's harder with a family, isn't it. Have you got kids?
B: One son, Kacper, fourteen. We live with my brother and his wife. I help him with maths, but now he needs a laptop for school, for the homework online, and with student loan, er, it is difficult. I am looking at second-hand.
A: Sorry, this might be a bit forward, but I actually refurbish old laptops. Clients replace them, I wipe them properly, new battery if it needs one, and I give them to families from the mosque, the kids' schools, that sort of thing. I've got two on the shelf at the moment. If it'd help, I'd happily sort one for Kacper. Is that alright to offer?
B: Really? That is very kind. I don't want to take something for free, though.
A: It's not really free. It'd just be sat on my shelf otherwise, if that makes sense.
B: Okay. Thank you. Maybe we can arrange through the study, I don't know how.
A: We'll ask them. What do you do when you're not studying?
B: I walk. Every evening, Sankey Valley trail. And a little rugby, Warrington Wolves, sometimes.
A: I walk too. Castle Hill, mostly, or the canal. I'm a bit obsessive about my steps.
B: And I have spreadsheet of all my marks. So I understand.
A: Ha. I've got ring binders, which you probably saw.
B: I saw. I thought, this man is organised. Your children, they are with you?
A: Every other weekend, and Wednesdays for tea. Zain's seventeen, Aleena's fourteen. They want my mum's dal every week, so I've learned it properly.
B: That is nice, the mother's recipe. My mother is still in Poland, alone now. I go every August. I worry, but she says she is fine. They always say fine.
A: They do. My dad's the same, he's seventy-nine. Lives with my brother, thank God, but he'll never tell you if something's wrong. I find out at his appointments.
B: Yes. It is the same everywhere, I think. Old people, they don't want to be trouble.
A: No. And then you're the one worrying at two in the morning, aren't you.
B: Exactly. Then you go to Mass, or for you, the mosque, and a little bit it is better.
A: It is, yes. It helps more than people think. Do you go every...
